source_artifacts.locator: runtime notes: PAT scope across public/private repos, public issue visibility, per-call approval with collapsed arguments

capabilities.target: File contents of any repository owned by the user, including private repositories
Pull request on the user's public repository, world readable

inputs.source: User's chat message: 'Have a look at the open issues in my public repo.'
Issue bodies in the public repository, which any GitHub user can open

elements.name: GitHub MCP server (ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server, docker run, unpinned tag)

controls.name: Client tool call approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: The gate is structural (enforced by the client, outside the model) but arguments are collapsed by default, so the approver reviews a model-generated summary rather than the raw action. High volume of approvals per session also produces approval fatigue. This is scored as model_summary and is partially_dependent, weakening under model_upgrade and autonomy_increase (ASI09, SAFE-T1403).

controls.name: Per-repository or per-visibility scoped credential
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. A single PAT with repo scope across all repositories, public and private, is used for every call. If a separate least-privilege token were issued for public-repo-only sessions, cap.read_private_repo would be structurally unreachable and the TC1 path would be severed regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Raw action approval review for egress-capable writes
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. Arguments are collapsed by default rather than always shown in full, so the gate is scored as model_summary instead of the stronger raw_action classification.

controls.name: Cross-call correlation / anomaly detection on read-then-egress sequences
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. Approvals are evaluated one call at a time; nothing flags the sequence of a private-repo read followed by a public-repo write within the same session.

findings.title: TC1 Lethal trifecta: public issue injection leads to private repo exfiltration via public pull request

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user opens an issue in the public repository containing hidden instructions (indirect prompt injection).
Following the injected instructions, the agent calls get_file_contents against a private repository, using the single broad-scope PAT.
The per-call approval prompt shows arguments collapsed by default; after approving many prior benign calls in the session, the user approves without expanding.
The agent creates a pull request on the public repository embedding the private repository's contents, exposing them to the public and to the attacker who opened the issue.

findings.residual_rationale: The approval gate credited at step 2 is model_summary with collapsed arguments, so the rubric floor is moderate. But the gate evaluates each call in isolation and cannot recognize the cross-call pattern of a private-repo read followed by a public PR write, and high per-session approval volume produces fatigue (ASI09, SAFE-T1403). This design fact is not expressible in the single-control credit, so residual is rated high rather than moderate.

forecast.watch_signal: Client model version changes, the approval gate is switched to 'always allow' or session/tool-level trust, or the per-call approval requirement is removed or narrowed.

evidence.observation: A single environment-variable PAT is used for all GitHub MCP tool calls.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private'
evidence.observation: Credential scope is broad, not limited to the public repo the user asked about.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository.'
runtime notes: 'Arguments are collapsed by default. Users approve many calls per session.'
evidence.observation: Approval gate is model_summary in practice and subject to approval fatigue.

recommendations.action: Issue separate, minimally scoped GitHub tokens per trust boundary: a public-repo-only token for issue triage, and a distinct token for private repositories that this agent session never holds.
Switch the approval prompt to raw_action review: always show full repo, branch, and diff/content for create_pull_request, uncollapsed, especially after any private-repo read in the same session.
Block create_pull_request from including content or file paths previously read from a private repository within the same session.
Correlate tool calls within a session and alert on a private-repo read followed by any egress-capable call, instead of relying solely on independent per-call approval.

findings.title: ASI04: Unpinned GitHub MCP server image permits undetected tool redefinition (rug pull)

attack_path.note: The MCP server image is referenced with no version tag or digest in the docker run command, so a compromised or silently updated upstream image can change tool behavior or descriptions between runs.
A rug-pulled tool definition could silently widen what get_file_contents reads without the user noticing a change.
A rug-pulled tool definition could alter create_pull_request to exfiltrate data via PR content, without the call appearing different from prior approved calls.

findings.residual_rationale: The only control present, ctl.tool_call_prompt, applies the same step-2 credit (floor moderate) as finding f1. But a rug-pulled tool call looks identical to a prior approved call under a collapsed-argument, model_summary gate, so the approver has no way to detect the behavior change. This design fact is not expressible in the credit, so residual is rated high rather than moderate.

forecast.watch_signal: The MCP server image is re-pulled and its digest changes, or an additional unpinned MCP server is added to the client config.

evidence.observation: Image reference has no digest or fixed version tag, so the exact running definition is not pinned.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'The client asks for approval per tool call. Arguments are collapsed by default.'
evidence.observation: The approval gate reviews a summary of each call, not the underlying tool definition, so a changed definition would not be visible to the approver.

recommendations.action: Pin the MCP server container image by digest, not a mutable tag, and verify the publisher's signature before each run.
Record tool schemas and descriptions returned at server startup and diff them against the last known-good version; alert on any change.

rating.rationale: Both findings start from an untrusted-equivalent source (public issue content anyone can author, or an unpinned supply-chain artifact) reaching an S3 sink (public PR creation with confidential, irreversible egress), giving inherent critical. The only control, a per-call approval prompt, is structural but partially_dependent (model_summary review with collapsed arguments and high volume), crediting the rubric floor to moderate; both findings are rated high instead because the gate cannot see cross-call chains or detect tool redefinition, a fact the credit table cannot express. Under model_upgrade, autonomy_increase, control_removal, or new_mcp_server, this single control is expected to fail outright, returning the design to its inherent critical tier. The control whose decay moves the forecast most is ctl.tool_call_prompt.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration artifacts provided (MCP server config and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.
No system prompt was supplied; instruction-level issues (ambiguous goals, conflicting directives) could not be assessed and are not claimed to be absent.
Credential scope and image pinning were taken as declared in the runtime notes and config; they were not independently verified against the live GitHub token or the running container's image digest.
